newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries open lower, fall sharply.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries open lower, fall sharply.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices opened lower on Friday amid deteriorated technical conditions and fell sharply in early trade, analysts said.

The market began its reversal on Thursday afternoon minutes after the Treasury annnounced the fairly strong results for its $10.0 billion 30-year bond auction. After moving to session highs immediately after that news, the market suddenly reversed itself. The benchmark 30-year bond yield closed above 6.50 percent for the first time since July 21.
The selling continued unabated on Friday morning.
At 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, the benchmark 30-year bond was priced at 97-16/32, down 18/32 from Thursday's close and yielding 6.56 percent.

"There's no news in particular," said Lee Youngdahl, bond market analyst at Aubrey G. Lanston. "It's bad positions basically. After the refunding, people are caught above the market and they're selling because they're losing money. They're trapped longs and longs have gotten very little satisfaction over the last week or so. They're bailing out."
No government economic reports are due during this session, analysts noted.

Poor technicals, supply from the Treasury's just completed $38.0 billion quarterly refunding, a weaker dollar and nervousness before next week's July retail sales and industrial production data all contributed to the market's jitters, analysts said.

"What's been going on in the last week is that in the second quarter you had the terrific secular story and you had the cyclical slowdown," said Neal Soss, managing director and senior advisor at Credit Suisse First Boston. "You had growth without inflation - the new secular story. And you had the relief of pressures of even a cyclical nature.
"That kind of combination is one that securities markets deserve to love," said Soss.
Soss said that while the secular story remains in place, cyclical pressures appear to be picking up.

The National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) report and U.S. employment report last Friday and retail and auto sales numbers this week point to firmer economic activity in the third quarter than in the second, he said.
Economists have widely anticipated that economic activity would pick up in the third quarter after second-quarter growth slowed from a brisk first quarter.
"Now what's happening is that the secular story is worth X number of basis points and the cyclical story was worth some basis points in addition to that," said Soss.
Soss said some of the basis points improvement related to the cyclical story are being reversed.
"And markets being markets, it's more noticeable when they go down than when they go up," he said.

A large West Coast fund was said to be selling $1.0 billion in bonds, according to analysts at Standard & Poor's MMS. Other hedge funds sold 10-years and there was talk of Japanese accounts selling five-year notes, they said.

At the short end of the maturity range, three- and six-month bill rates were each up one basis point to 5.17 percent and 5.24 percent, respectively. Year bill rates were up five basis points to 5.28 percent.
After the first hour of trading, two-year Treasury notes were down 3/32 to 99-26/32, yielding 5.98 percent.
Five-year notes were down 8/32 to 99-6/32 to yield 6.19 percent.
Ten-year notes were priced at 98-19/32, down 17/32 to yield 6.32 percent.
((-- North American Treasury Desk, 212-859-1679 ))
